newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.N. and Zaire discuss refugee repatriation.
newsitem.headline: U.N. and Zaire discuss refugee repatriation.

text.p: The U.N. High Commissioner for refugees, Sadako Ogata, said in Zaire on Friday she was working with the government on ways to repatriate the remaining Rwandan Hutu refugees trapped by war in the east.
But she said there was no longer any need for international military intervention to protect the refugees, even if this had been the case in December.

Ogata, who has called for a political and security solution to the Tutsi-led revolt in east Zaire, arrived in Kinshasa on Friday as fighting escalated in the war zone, where an estimated 300,000 refugees are clustered at various sites.
"The refugees have to go back home," she told reporters after meeting Foreign Minister Mende Omalanga.
"We are working on the modalities with the governement. In theory, there are two ways of repatriating the refugees, by plane or by road through safety corridors," she said.

The Rwandan Hutus trapped in different parts of the war zone fled west with hardline Hutu gunmen after more than 500,000 of their fellow Hutus opted to return home following attacks on their long-standing camps in the east in December.
Tutsi-led rebels, who hold towns and territory in the east, have pushed west despite a January 20 army counter-offensive.
Military officials in Kinshasa said on Friday that the army had hit back, recapturing the towns of Watsa and Shabunda but rebels said they were firmly in control.
A senior defence official and sources at army headquarters in Kinshasa also said the armed forces had bombarded rebel positions from the air around Walikale, which the army says it holds.

"The fighting at Watsa was extremely heavy. But we took them by surprise and Watsa was completely retaken overnight. There were 800 rebels killed," the official said. He said Shabunda was retaken on Thursday.

Church sources in the region said on Wednesday that many of the rebels, who launched their revolt in October, had passed through Shabunda and were heading toward Kindu, where the army concentrated troops for its counter-offensive.
There was no independent confirmation of the status of the towns, although independent sources in the region confirmed Walikale had been bombarded from the air on Thursday.

Rwandan Hutu refugee camps along the road from Walikale to Kisangani, headquarters for the army counter-offensive, were tense, aid workers said. They reported 70 wounded soldiers arriving at Lubutu hospital, about 200 km (125 miles) from Kisangani.

Relief groups pulled non-essential staff out of Lubutu on Friday and made contingency plans to evacuate remaining staff. The World Food Programme in Nairobi said Zairean troops had stopped six local aid workers leaving and had maltreated them.

But Ogata played down the need for an international force to protect refugees, an idea that won support last year but failed to get off the ground. "A military intervention would have been necessary in December, but not now," she said.
Ogata was to visit the nearby refugee camp at Tingi Tingi on Saturday. It was not clear whether the visit would go ahead.
The U.N. Children's Fund (UNICEF) estimated that 772 of the 120,000 refugees in Tingi Tingi had died from hunger or disease since February 3. More than 400 were children under five.

Mobutu, who seized power in 1965, was expected home from Europe by the weekend after tests following prostate surgery. He travelled via Morocco, whose troops helped him crush 1970s rebellions in Shaba, but he denied seeking military help there.
